# Implement block: Depth Field Gallery (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Depth Field Gallery" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

Cards floating in space on a white screen, scattered in depth so the near ones are large and the far ones tiny, and in each view one card fills most of the width just off the middle while a dozen smaller ones float around it out to the edges. The cards make up an invented identity: some forty portraits, profiles, fashion shots and busts printed in black and white or black on lime, lime cards with a cluster of black dots of many sizes, near-black cards with icons drawn in white dots (a magnifier, a cross of arrows, a figure, a basket), dark cards with two glassy rows each led by a lime dot, framed posters with two lines of type over a portrait ("Where depth meets focus", "Light finds its level", "Still air, clear sight"), and an "aloft" wordmark with a square of lime dots. Each card is turned a little in space. Tiny tracked capitals sit along the top ("Aloft Studio", "Depth Field" and the card's number, "07 / 49"); at the bottom the card in view is named, a small note in capitals over its title, beside a small switch with a lime knob. The switch turns the scene to near black, the dark cards keeping a faint edge.

**Motion.** A hundred and sixty cards, dealt from the forty-nine designs, float through a 64-unit tunnel that repeats behind itself (a unit is about a card's width), each turned by up to 0.14 rad about the vertical axis, 0.1 about the horizontal and 0.035 in its plane, and swaying gently, seen through a lens whose focal length is 95% of the screen's width. Every fourth card, the stops taking the designs in an order that visits all of them before repeating, floats within 0.8 units of the middle across and 1.3 up and down as a stop for the camera; the rest are scattered up to 3 units across and 4.8 up and down, clear of the middle. To frame a card the camera stands far enough back for it to fill 62% of the width, up to 7% of the width and 5% of the height off the middle. Cards fade in between 12 and 9 units away and out between 0.8 and 0.35 units. By itself the camera flies in on the first card from 3 units back over 1.5 s while the cards fade in, then flies on from stop to stop: each flight takes 0.95 s on an ease-in-out curve (0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) to the next stop ahead, arriving 0.2 units short and a little to one side, and the camera drifts in the rest of the way over 1.1 s while it holds for 0.9 s, the cards around sliding past by depth; every sixth flight the lights turn over on the way, the other scene spreading from the switch. As each card arrives its number and caption cross over in 0.35 s, the new ones rising 8 pt into place while the last ones rise away. Dragging up flies on and dragging down flies back, 0.014 units per pt, and dragging sideways pans 0.006 units per pt, the cards sliding past each other by depth; on release the camera flies to the stop nearest where the drag was heading 0.25 s ahead, on a spring (duration 750 ms, damping ratio 0.9) that carries the finger's speed. Tapping a card flies the camera to frame it on a spring (duration 950 ms, damping ratio 0.92) with a light haptic. Tapping the switch turns the lights over with a selection haptic: the other scene spreads in a circle from the switch to the far corner over 0.9 s on an ease-in-out curve (0.77, 0, 0.175, 1), the labels changing ink exactly at its edge, and the knob slides across. A touch pauses the flight from stop to stop for 3 s. Under reduced motion the camera does not fly by itself, nothing sways, drifts or flies in, the lights cross-fade in 250 ms and the camera moves in 250 ms without springs. Every photo is fetched at 480 by 600 px for the field; the card at the current stop and the one at the next are fetched again at 1000 by 1250 px and fade in over the smaller copy, the last four kept.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [DepthFieldGalleryDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Animations/DepthFieldGallery/DepthFieldGalleryDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [DepthFieldGallery.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Animations/DepthFieldGallery/DepthFieldGallery.swift)
- [DepthFieldGalleryCards.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Animations/DepthFieldGallery/DepthFieldGalleryCards.swift)
- [DepthFieldGalleryEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Animations/DepthFieldGallery/DepthFieldGalleryEngine.swift)
- [DepthFieldGalleryFaces.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Animations/DepthFieldGallery/DepthFieldGalleryFaces.swift)
- [DepthFieldGalleryMotion.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Animations/DepthFieldGallery/DepthFieldGalleryMotion.swift)

### Used by the demo only

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
